x: ICT joins three ideas. Information is processed, meaningful data: a list of marks is data, but ‘Ali got the highest marks in Class 9’ is information. Communication is the transfer of that information between people or machines, by text, voice, image or video. Technology is the set of tools that makes the first two fast and cheap. ICT is wider than IT (Information Technology) because it also includes telecommunication: mobile networks, radio, television and the internet. An ICT system always follows the same cycle: input, processing, output, storage, and often communication to another system.

Hardware is any part of an ICT system you can touch. It is easiest to understand by the job each device does in the processing cycle. Input devices bring data in, the processor (CPU) works on it using fast temporary memory (RAM), output devices show or print results, storage devices keep data when the power is off, and communication devices connect the system to others. A smartphone contains all five groups in one body: touch screen and camera (input), processor and RAM (processing), screen and speaker (output), internal flash storage (storage) and Wi-Fi, 4G and Bluetooth radios (communication).

Software is the set of instructions that tells hardware what to do. System software manages the machine itself: the operating system (Windows, Android, macOS, Linux, iOS) controls files, memory, devices and users, while utility programs such as antivirus, backup and disk cleanup keep it healthy. Application software helps the user complete a task: Word for documents, Excel for calculations, Chrome for browsing, JazzCash for payments. Device drivers are small pieces of system software that let the operating system talk to a specific printer, scanner or graphics card. Software can be proprietary (Microsoft Office, paid licence), free (Google Docs, free to use but owned by a company) or open source (LibreOffice, source code anyone can study).

A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources such as a printer or an internet connection. Networks are grouped mainly by the area they cover. A Personal Area Network (PAN) links devices around one person, such as earbuds connected by Bluetooth. A Local Area Network (LAN) covers one building or campus, like the computer lab of a school, and is usually owned by that organisation. A Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) covers a city. A Wide Area Network (WAN) connects sites across cities or countries, such as a bank linking all its branches. The internet is the largest WAN: a global network of networks that uses common rules called protocols (TCP/IP). Devices connect by cable (Ethernet, fibre) or wirelessly (Wi-Fi, 4G/5G).

Storage keeps data when the power is switched off. Local storage is inside or attached to your own device: the hard disk of a laptop, the phone’s internal memory or a USB drive. It works without internet and you control it physically, but it can be lost, stolen or damaged. Cloud storage keeps your files on servers owned by a provider such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive or Dropbox, and you reach them through the internet. It can be opened from any device and makes sharing easy, but it needs an internet connection and depends on a strong account password. RAM is not storage in this sense: it is volatile and loses its content when power is lost. Storage is measured in bytes: 1 KB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MB = 1,024 KB, 1 GB = 1,024 MB, 1 TB = 1,024 GB.

t: Lecture 1: ICT Fundamentals: Hardware, Software, Networks and Storage
x: What ICT means, the four building blocks of every ICT system (hardware, software, networks, storage), and the difference between local and cloud storage, with examples from a Bhimber computer lab. Every time a student in Bhimber sends a WhatsApp voice note, checks a result on a board website or prints an assignment at a photocopy shop, an ICT system is at work. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is the combination of devices, programs and networks that let people create, store, process, share and receive information. Computer science studies how these systems are built; ICT as a General Education subject focuses on using them well. This first lecture gives you the vocabulary that the rest of the course depends on: once you can name the parts of an ICT system, you can reason about why a file will not open, why the internet is slow in the lab, or where your photos are actually kept. ICT = information + communication + technology, wider than IT. Every ICT system has hardware, software, networks and storage. System software runs the machine; application software helps the user. Networks are classified by area: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN and the internet. Local storage works offline; cloud storage works anywhere with internet.
Central Processing Unit; carries out instructions and calculations.
Random Access Memory; fast temporary memory that is cleared when power is off.
System software that manages hardware, files and applications.
Software that lets the operating system control a specific device.
An agreed set of rules for communication, such as TCP/IP or HTTP.
The amount of data a connection can carry per second, measured in Mbps.
Saving files on a provider’s internet servers instead of your own device.
An external device connected to a computer, such as a printer.
The set of technologies used to create, store, process, transmit and receive information, including computers, software, networks and telecommunication.
The physical, tangible components of an ICT system.
A set of programs and instructions that direct hardware to perform tasks.
Two or more connected devices that share data and resources.

ICT changes how students learn and how institutions manage teaching. Learning Management Systems such as Google Classroom and Moodle distribute material and collect assignments. Video lectures, digital libraries and online courses let a student in Bhimber learn from teachers anywhere in the world. Administration also depends on ICT: admissions, fee challans, attendance and results are increasingly handled online. The Higher Education Commission’s digital library gives university students access to research journals that would otherwise be unaffordable.

Businesses use ICT to sell, manage and communicate. Point-of-sale systems record every sale and update stock automatically. Spreadsheets and accounting software track income and expenses. Social media pages and WhatsApp Business let a small shop reach customers without paying for a physical advertisement. E-commerce platforms such as Daraz allow a seller in a small city to deliver across Pakistan. Freelancing platforms have made Pakistan one of the largest sources of online freelancers, with young people earning from graphic design, writing and programming.

E-governance means delivering government services and information through ICT. It reduces queues, paperwork and opportunities for bribery, because each step is recorded. In Pakistan, NADRA issues identity cards through a national database, FBR’s IRIS portal lets citizens file tax returns online, the Pakistan Citizen’s Portal allows complaints to be lodged and tracked from a phone, and many provinces offer online driving licence verification and land record services.

t: L2: ICT in healthcare and digital media
x: Hospitals use ICT for patient records, digital imaging, laboratory reports and appointment systems. Telemedicine connects patients in remote areas to doctors in big cities by video call. In digital media, news, entertainment and advertising have moved online: people now watch YouTube and stream dramas instead of only waiting for a TV schedule, and anyone with a phone can publish content. This brings opportunities for creators but also spreads misinformation quickly, a topic we return to in Lecture 12.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is software that performs tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech, translating languages or recommending videos. Machine learning, a branch of AI, lets software learn patterns from data instead of following only fixed rules. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects everyday objects such as meters, cameras and water pumps to the internet so they can send data and be controlled remotely. Cloud computing provides computing power, storage and software over the internet on demand, so a small business can rent a server instead of buying one. 5G is the fifth generation of mobile networks, offering much higher speed and lower delay than 4G, which supports IoT devices and real-time video.

t: Lecture 2: Scope of ICT and Emerging Technologies
x: How ICT is used in education, business, governance, healthcare and digital media, and an introduction to AI, IoT, cloud computing and 5G with Pakistani examples. In Lecture 1 we looked inside an ICT system. Now we step back and ask where these systems are used and where they are going. Almost every sector in Pakistan has been reshaped by ICT in the last fifteen years: students submit assignments on Google Classroom, shopkeepers accept Easypaisa, patients book doctors on Marham and citizens verify property records online. At the same time, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things are moving from research labs into ordinary phones and homes. Understanding this scope helps you choose a career, spot opportunities for local businesses and recognise the risks that come with new technology. ICT is used across education, business, governance, health and media. E-governance makes services faster and more transparent. AI learns from data; IoT connects objects; cloud rents computing; 5G speeds up networks. Each technology brings both opportunities and risks. Local businesses can grow using simple, low-cost ICT tools.
Delivery of government services and information through ICT.
Buying and selling goods or services over the internet.
Software that performs tasks needing human-like intelligence.
A type of AI in which systems learn patterns from data.
Internet of Things: everyday objects connected to the internet.
Software as a Service: applications used through a browser on subscription or free.
The delay between sending and receiving data over a network.
Providing medical consultation remotely using ICT.
The range of fields and activities in which ICT is applied.
A new technology that is developing quickly and expected to have a large social or economic effect.
On-demand delivery of computing resources such as storage, servers and software over the internet.

t: L3: How a search engine works
x: A search engine does three jobs. Crawling: automated programs called crawlers or spiders follow links from page to page and download their content. Indexing: the content is analysed and stored in a giant index, like the index at the back of a book, that records which words appear on which pages. Ranking: when you type a query, the engine searches its index and orders the matching pages using hundreds of signals such as relevance of words, quality of the site, links from other pages, your location and freshness. Results marked ‘Sponsored’ or ‘Ad’ are paid placements, not necessarily the best answers.

Good searching begins with good keywords. Remove filler words, keep the key concepts and add a word that describes the type of source you need. Instead of ‘what are the effects of mobile phones on students in Pakistan’, search ‘mobile phone use academic performance Pakistan study’. Use specific terms (‘literacy rate’ rather than ‘education level’), try synonyms when results are poor and add a year for recent data. Searching is iterative: read the first results, learn the correct terminology they use, then refine your query.

Operators are symbols or words that give the search engine exact instructions. Quotation marks search for an exact phrase. A minus sign excludes a word. site: limits results to one website or domain type, such as site:gov.pk for Pakistani government pages or site:edu.pk for universities. filetype: finds a specific format such as PDF or PPTX. OR (in capitals) finds either term. intitle: requires a word in the page title. Operators can be combined: “literacy rate” site:pbs.gov.pk filetype:pdf.

t: L3: Evaluating sources: the CRAAP test
x: Before using a source, check five things. Currency: when was it published or updated, and is that recent enough for your topic? Relevance: does it answer your question at the right level? Authority: who wrote it, and what are their qualifications or organisation? Accuracy: is it supported by evidence, data or references, and do other reliable sources agree? Purpose: is it written to inform, or to sell, persuade or entertain? Official domains such as .gov.pk and .edu.pk, peer-reviewed journals and recognised news organisations are usually more reliable than anonymous blogs, forums or social media posts.

t: L3: Google, Bing and specialised tools
x: Google has the largest share of searches in Pakistan and strong local results. Bing, built into Microsoft Edge and Windows, offers similar operators, image search and AI-assisted answers through Copilot. Results differ because each engine has its own index and ranking. For academic work, use Google Scholar to find research papers and see how many times they are cited, the HEC Digital Library for journal access through your university, and official statistics sites such as the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. AI chat tools can summarise information but may produce confident mistakes, so always verify facts in an original source.

t: Lecture 3: Search Engines and Web Research
x: How search engines crawl, index and rank pages, how to write effective keywords and use search operators, and how to judge whether a source is reliable. Most students search the way they speak: they type a full question and click the first result. That works for simple facts, but university assignments need accurate, citable sources. A search engine is not a list of truths; it is a ranking of pages that its software predicts you want. This lecture explains what happens behind the search box, teaches the operators that turn a vague query into a precise one, and gives you a simple test to decide whether a page deserves to be in your assignment. Search engines crawl, index and rank pages. Effective searches use focused keywords, not full questions. Operators such as quotes, site: and filetype: narrow results. Use the CRAAP test before trusting a source. Use Google Scholar and official sites for academic work and verify AI answers.
A program that automatically visits web pages by following links.
The search engine’s database of words and the pages that contain them.
The words typed into a search engine.
A symbol or word that refines a search, such as quotes or site:.
The address of a website, such as hec.gov.pk.
A reference that tells readers where information came from.
Checking of research by other experts before publication.
Search Engine Results Page.
A software system that finds and ranks web pages that match a user’s query.
The systematic process of finding, evaluating and using information from the internet.
A source that is current, written by a qualified author, supported by evidence and published for an informative purpose.

An email address has two parts separated by @: the user name and the domain, for example ali.khan@gmail.com or registrar@uob.edu.pk. When you click Send, your email client (Gmail, Outlook) passes the message to your provider’s outgoing mail server using the SMTP protocol. That server finds the recipient’s mail server from the domain name and delivers it. The recipient’s app then downloads or displays it using IMAP or POP3. Email is asynchronous: the receiver does not need to be online at the same moment, which makes it ideal for formal records.

t: L4: To, CC, BCC and attachments
x: To is for the main person who must read and act on the email. CC (carbon copy) is for people who should be kept informed; everyone can see who was CC’d. BCC (blind carbon copy) hides recipients from each other, which protects privacy when emailing a large group, such as a teacher writing to all parents. Attachments add files; keep them small (Gmail limits attachments to 25 MB and offers a Drive link for larger files), name them clearly such as Assignment2_AliKhan.pdf and prefer PDF so formatting does not change. Reply answers only the sender; Reply all answers everyone in To and CC, so use it carefully. Forward sends the message to someone new.

t: L4: Structure of a formal email
x: A formal email has six parts. Subject line: short and specific, such as ‘Request for leave on 12 March – BSCS Section A’. Greeting: ‘Dear Sir/Madam’, ‘Dear Dr. Ahmed’ or ‘Respected Ma’am’. Opening line: who you are and why you are writing. Body: the details in short paragraphs, with dates and reference numbers. Closing: a polite request or thanks, such as ‘I would be grateful for your consideration.’ Signature: full name, roll number or designation, department and contact number. Avoid SMS language, all capital letters, emojis and slang in formal emails.

Reply within one or two working days, proofread before sending and check that attachments are actually attached. Do not forward chain messages. Use a professional address, ideally firstname.lastname rather than a nickname. Organise your inbox with labels or folders and archive old messages. Be alert to phishing: emails that pretend to be from a bank, university or courier and ask you to click a link or share a password or OTP. Check the sender’s real address, hover over links before clicking and never share a PIN or OTP by email.

Video meetings are synchronous: everyone joins at the same time. Google Meet works in a browser with a Google account and integrates with Google Calendar and Classroom. Microsoft Teams combines chat, meetings and file sharing and is common in universities that use Microsoft 365. Zoom is widely used for webinars and large classes. All three support screen sharing, chat, raising a hand, recording (with permission) and breakout rooms in some plans. Good meeting etiquette: join on time, keep the microphone muted when not speaking, use a real name, turn the camera on when asked, use the chat for questions and stay focused.

t: Lecture 4: Email and Formal Digital Communication
x: Using Gmail and Outlook professionally: To, CC, BCC, attachments, formal email structure and etiquette, and running video meetings on Google Meet, Teams and Zoom. WhatsApp is perfect for friends, but universities, employers and government offices still communicate formally by email. Your first contact with a teacher about a missed quiz, an application for an internship or a complaint to a department will usually be an email, and its tone will shape how people see you. Video conferencing has also become part of normal study and work since online classes became common. This lecture teaches the tools and, more importantly, the manners of professional digital communication. Email is asynchronous and leaves a written record. Use To for action, CC for information and BCC for privacy. A formal email has subject, greeting, opening, body, closing and signature. Watch for phishing and never share OTPs or passwords. Meet, Teams and Zoom need good etiquette: mute, real name, punctuality.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, used to send email.
Protocol that keeps email synchronised on the server across devices.
Carbon copy: an additional visible recipient.
Blind carbon copy: a hidden recipient.
A file sent along with an email.
A fraudulent message designed to steal passwords or money.
Communication in real time, such as a video call.
Communication not in real time, such as email.
Electronic mail: a method of exchanging digital messages and files over the internet.
Accepted rules of polite and professional behaviour when writing emails.

Microsoft Word is a desktop application, part of Microsoft Office or Microsoft 365, and also runs in a browser as Word for the web. Google Docs runs in a browser, saves automatically to Google Drive and is free with a Google account. Both handle the same core tasks. Character formatting changes text: font, size, bold, italic, underline, colour. Paragraph formatting changes whole paragraphs: alignment (left, centre, right, justify), line spacing, spacing before and after, indentation, bullets and numbering. For academic work, a clean font such as Calibri, Times New Roman or Arial at 11–12 point with 1.15–1.5 line spacing is standard.

A style is a saved set of formatting with a name, such as Normal, Title, Heading 1 and Heading 2. When you apply Heading 1 to every chapter title, three things happen: all chapters look identical, changing the style once updates every heading, and the software understands the document’s structure. That structure powers the Navigation Pane in Word and the document outline in Docs, which let you jump to any section, and it is required for an automatic table of contents. Use Heading 1 for main sections, Heading 2 for subsections and Heading 3 for smaller parts; never skip levels.

t: L5: Page layout: numbers, headers, footers and breaks
x: Page numbers are inserted from Insert → Page Number (Word) or Insert → Page numbers (Docs) and update automatically. Headers and footers repeat on every page and usually hold the document title, course code or student name. A page break (Ctrl + Enter) starts a new page cleanly instead of pressing Enter many times. A section break in Word lets different parts of a document have different layouts, for example no page number on the title page, Roman numerals for the contents pages and Arabic numerals from the introduction onward. ‘Different first page’ hides the header on the title page.

t: L5: Table of contents, tables and images
x: Once headings use styles, insert a table of contents from References → Table of Contents (Word) or Insert → Table of contents (Docs). When headings or page numbers change, click Update Table. Tables organise data in rows and columns: insert them from Insert → Table, add a header row, use table styles and keep tables simple. Images are inserted from Insert → Pictures; set text wrapping (In line with text is safest), resize from the corner to keep proportions and add a caption (References → Insert Caption) such as ‘Figure 1: Bhimber Mart sales chart’. Only use images you have the right to use.

Academic writing must credit sources. Word’s References → Insert Citation stores sources and creates a bibliography automatically in styles such as APA or IEEE; Docs offers Tools → Citations. Footnotes add notes at the bottom of a page. For group work, comments let reviewers suggest changes without editing the text, and Track Changes (Word) or Suggesting mode (Docs) records every edit so the author can accept or reject it. Sharing in Docs or OneDrive uses links with Viewer, Commenter or Editor permission. Finally, export to PDF (File → Save As → PDF, or File → Download → PDF) before submitting, so formatting cannot change on another computer.

t: Lecture 5: Microsoft Word and Google Docs
x: Producing professional documents: formatting, styles and headings, page numbers, headers and footers, automatic table of contents, tables, images, references, comments and sharing. A word processor is the tool you will use most often at university: for assignments, lab reports, project documentation, applications and your CV. Most students use Word like a typewriter, pressing Enter repeatedly to move to a new page and making headings bold by hand. That makes documents hard to edit and impossible to navigate. This lecture shows how professionals work: they let styles control the appearance, let the software number pages and build the contents table, and use collaboration features so a group can work on one file without emailing versions back and forth. Use styles, not manual bold, for headings. Heading styles enable navigation and automatic contents. Page numbers, headers, footers and breaks control layout. Tables, images and captions present information clearly. Use citations, comments, sharing and PDF export for academic work.
A named set of formatting applied to text, such as Heading 1.
A pre-designed document used as a starting point.
A divider that allows different page layouts in one document.
Area at the top or bottom of every page.
A feature that records edits for review.
A numbered label for a table or figure.
A list of sources cited in a document.
Tool that copies formatting from one place to another.
Application software used to create, edit, format and print text documents.
An automatically generated list of headings with page numbers.
A reference within the text to the source of information.

A workbook is the whole file; it contains one or more worksheets (tabs). Each sheet is a grid of columns labelled with letters (A, B, C …) and rows labelled with numbers (1, 2, 3 …). Their intersection is a cell, identified by its address, such as B4. A group of cells is a range, written with a colon, such as B2:B21. Cells hold text (labels), numbers, dates or formulas. The Name Box shows the selected cell’s address and the Formula Bar shows what the cell really contains. Excel is part of Microsoft Office; Google Sheets is free in a browser and saves to Drive automatically.

Every formula begins with an equals sign. It can use numbers, cell addresses and operators: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) and ^ (power). Spreadsheets follow the mathematical order of operations, BODMAS/PEMDAS: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So =2+3*4 gives 14 while =(2+3)*4 gives 20. Using cell addresses instead of typed numbers is what makes a spreadsheet useful: =C2*D2 calculates a line total and updates automatically when the price in C2 changes.

A function is a built-in formula with a name and arguments in brackets. SUM adds a range: =SUM(E2:E21). AVERAGE finds the mean, MIN and MAX the smallest and largest values, COUNT counts cells with numbers and COUNTA counts non-empty cells. COUNTIF counts cells meeting a condition, such as =COUNTIF(F2:F21,"Low stock"). IF makes a decision: =IF(D2<10,"Low stock","OK") shows ‘Low stock’ when the quantity is below 10. Text in formulas must be in straight double quotes. Functions can be combined, for example =IF(E2>AVERAGE(E$2:E$21),"Above average","Below").

When you copy a formula down a column with the fill handle (the small square at the bottom-right of a selected cell), the cell addresses change relative to the new position: =C2*D2 in row 2 becomes =C3*D3 in row 3. This is a relative reference and is usually what you want. Sometimes a formula must always point to one fixed cell, such as a tax rate or discount stored in H1. Add dollar signs to make it absolute: =E2*$H$1. Press F4 in Excel to toggle dollar signs. Mixed references ($H1 or H$1) fix only the column or only the row.

t: L6: Sorting, filtering, formatting and charts
x: Sorting rearranges rows by a column, for example highest sales first; always select the whole table so rows stay together. Filtering (Data → Filter) shows only rows that meet a condition, such as category ‘Grocery’, without deleting anything. Conditional formatting colours cells automatically, for example red for quantity below 10. Number formats display values as currency (Rs), percentages or dates. Charts turn numbers into pictures: a column or bar chart compares items, a line chart shows change over time and a pie chart shows parts of a whole (use it only for a few categories that add to 100%). Every chart needs a title and labelled axes.

t: Lecture 6: Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets
x: Spreadsheet basics: cells, ranges and formulas; SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, IF and relative vs absolute references; sorting, filtering, conditional formatting and charts, using a Bhimber Mart sales sheet. A spreadsheet is a grid that calculates. Shopkeepers use it to track stock, teachers to compile results, accountants to prepare budgets and researchers to analyse survey data. The power of a spreadsheet is that formulas recalculate instantly when any number changes, so you can ask ‘what if?’ questions. In this lecture we build a sales sheet for Bhimber Mart, a fictional store in the main bazaar, and use it to learn the formulas and tools that cover most everyday spreadsheet work. A workbook holds worksheets made of cells with addresses. Formulas start with = and follow the order of operations. SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTIF and IF cover most daily tasks. Relative references change when copied; absolute ($) references do not. Sort, filter, conditional formatting and charts turn data into decisions.
The intersection of a row and a column, such as B3.
A rectangular group of cells, such as A1:C10.
An expression beginning with = that calculates a value.
A built-in formula such as SUM or IF.
A value or range supplied inside a function’s brackets.
Small square used to copy formulas to adjacent cells.
A cell reference fixed with $ signs, such as $H$1.
Formatting that changes automatically based on cell values.
Application software that organises data in rows and columns and performs calculations using formulas.
A spreadsheet file containing one or more worksheets.
A graphical representation of spreadsheet data.

Microsoft PowerPoint (desktop, web and mobile) and Google Slides (browser, free) both organise a presentation as a sequence of slides. Each slide is built from a layout, such as Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content or Section Header, which contains placeholders for text, images and charts. A theme applies consistent colours, fonts and backgrounds to all slides. The Slide Master (View → Slide Master) controls the design of every layout at once, for example adding a university logo to all slides. Views include Normal for editing, Slide Sorter for reordering and Slide Show for presenting.

Good slide design follows a few principles. Contrast: dark text on a light background or the reverse, so it can be read from the back of the room on an old projector. Alignment: line up text and images along invisible edges. Repetition: keep fonts, colours and title positions consistent. Proximity: place related items together. White space: leave empty space so the slide breathes. Use sans-serif fonts such as Calibri, Arial or Segoe UI, at least 28 point for body text and 36–44 for titles. Limit each slide to one main idea and about six lines of text; the ‘6×6 guideline’ suggests no more than six bullets of six words each.

t: L7: Visuals: images, charts and diagrams
x: People remember pictures better than text. Use high-quality images that support the message, not decoration, and only images you are allowed to use (PowerPoint’s stock images or free licence sources). Charts should be simple: one message per chart, a clear title stating the takeaway such as ‘Grocery sales doubled in Ramadan’, and labels large enough to read. Charts can be inserted from Excel or created in Slides from Sheets. SmartArt (PowerPoint) or diagrams (Slides) show processes, cycles and hierarchies, for example the information processing cycle. Icons can replace words for simple ideas.

A transition is the effect between slides; an animation moves an object on a slide. Used sparingly, animation can reveal bullets one at a time so the audience listens instead of reading ahead, or show the steps of a process. Overused, it distracts and wastes time. Choose one subtle transition such as Fade for the whole presentation and use animations only when they explain something, for example ‘Appear’ for each step of a flowchart. Avoid sound effects and spinning or bouncing effects in academic presentations.

Speaker notes are written below each slide in the Notes pane and are visible only to the presenter in Presenter View, which also shows the next slide and a timer. Write the points you will say, examples and transitions, so the slide itself can stay short. Rehearse aloud with a timer; a common rule is about one to two minutes per slide. During delivery, face the audience rather than the screen, speak slowly and clearly, point to what matters, and finish with a summary slide and invite questions. Before presenting on another computer, export a PDF backup and embed fonts or use standard ones.

t: Lecture 7: Microsoft PowerPoint and Google Slides
x: Designing and delivering effective presentations: slide layouts, themes, readable fonts, images and charts, restrained transitions, speaker notes, presenter view and the principles of good slides. Presentations are part of almost every university course, job interview and business meeting. Software makes it easy to fill slides with text, colours and spinning animations, but that is exactly what makes many presentations hard to follow. A slide is a visual aid for a speaker, not a document to be read. In this lecture we learn the tools of PowerPoint and Google Slides, and the design and delivery principles that make an audience listen. Slides support the speaker; they are not documents. Use layouts, themes and the Slide Master for consistency. Follow contrast, alignment, repetition, proximity and white space. Use visuals and animations only when they explain something. Write speaker notes, rehearse with a timer and keep a PDF backup.
An arrangement of placeholders on a slide.
A box on a layout that holds text, images or charts.
A set of colours, fonts and effects applied to all slides.
The top-level slide that controls the design of all layouts.
A visual effect when moving from one slide to the next.
A visual effect applied to an object on a slide.
Notes for the presenter that the audience does not see.
A view showing notes, timer and next slide to the presenter.
Application software used to create a sequence of slides for displaying information to an audience.
Arranging elements so the most important information is noticed first.
Practising a presentation aloud with timing before delivering it.

Google Drive gives 15 GB free shared across Gmail, Drive and Google Photos, and integrates with Docs, Sheets, Slides and Classroom. Microsoft OneDrive gives 5 GB free (more with a Microsoft 365 or university account) and integrates with Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Windows File Explorer. Dropbox gives 2 GB free on its basic plan and is known for simple, reliable sync across devices. All three offer desktop and mobile apps that sync a local folder with the cloud, so a file edited on the lab computer appears on your phone. Free storage limits change over time, so check the provider’s current plan.

t: L8: Sync, version history and offline access
x: Sync means keeping the same files identical on several devices and the cloud. When you change a file on one device, the sync client uploads the change and other devices download it. Version history keeps earlier versions so you can restore yesterday’s copy if you overwrite something by mistake: in Google Docs use File → Version history, and in Drive or OneDrive right-click a file → Version history. Files can be made available offline so you can work during internet outages; changes upload when the connection returns. Deleted files go to the Bin/Recycle bin and can usually be restored for about 30 days.

Cloud sharing sends a link instead of a file copy, so everyone sees the latest version. Each person can be given a role: Viewer (can only see), Commenter (can see and comment) or Editor (can change, and by default share). Link sharing can be Restricted (only people added by name), limited to your organisation (for example everyone with a university account) or ‘Anyone with the link’. The safest default is Restricted or ‘Anyone with the link – Viewer’. Never give Editor access to people who do not need it, and remove access when a project ends. Owners can also prevent editors from re-sharing and disable downloading for viewers.

t: L8: Folder structure and file naming
x: A folder structure is a hierarchy that matches how you think about your work, for example University → Semester 1 → ICT → Lectures / Labs / Assignments / Exams. Keep it shallow (three or four levels) and consistent across subjects. A file naming convention makes files easy to sort and find: include what, who and when, avoid spaces and special characters, and use dates in YYYY-MM-DD format so files sort in order. Examples: ICT_Lab03_AliKhan_2026-03-14.docx, ICT_Assignment2_v2_AliKhan.pdf. Avoid names like ‘final final new.docx’.

Microsoft OneNote organises notes into notebooks, sections and pages, like a ring binder; it accepts typed text, handwriting, images, audio and web clippings, and syncs through OneDrive. Evernote organises notes into notebooks and tags and offers powerful search, including text inside images on some plans. Google Keep offers quick notes and checklists. Digital notes are searchable and backed up, but only if you organise them. The 3-2-1 backup rule says: keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage (for example laptop and USB drive), with 1 copy off-site (the cloud).

t: Lecture 8: Cloud Storage and Digital Note-Taking
x: Google Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox compared; sharing permissions; folder structures and file naming conventions; Evernote and OneNote for notes; and the 3-2-1 backup rule. Students lose work every semester: a USB drive is left in a computer lab, a phone is stolen, a laptop hard disk fails the night before a deadline. Cloud storage and good file habits prevent almost all of these disasters. In Lecture 1 we met cloud storage as an idea; now we use it properly. We compare the main services, learn to share files safely, design folders that make sense a year later, take organised digital notes and build a backup routine that would survive losing any single device. Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox store and sync files in the cloud. Version history and the Bin recover mistakes. Share with the least privilege needed; prefer Restricted links. Use shallow folder structures and consistent naming with dates. Use OneNote/Evernote for notes and follow the 3-2-1 backup rule.
Automatically keeping files identical across devices and the cloud.

c: Lecture 9 · ICT in Education and LMS
x: E-learning is learning supported or delivered through electronic devices and the internet. Synchronous learning happens in real time, such as a live Google Meet class. Asynchronous learning lets students study at their own time, such as recorded lectures, reading material and discussion forums. Blended learning (hybrid) combines face-to-face classes with online activities, for example lectures in class and quizzes on the LMS. A flipped classroom asks students to watch the lecture at home and use class time for problem-solving and discussion. Mobile learning (m-learning) uses phones, which is the main device for many students in Pakistan.

c: Lecture 9 · ICT in Education and LMS
x: A Learning Management System (LMS) is software that delivers, tracks and manages courses. Teachers upload material, create assignments and quizzes, grade work and send announcements; students view content, submit assignments, take quizzes, participate in forums and see their grades. Google Classroom is simple and free with a Google account and links with Drive, Docs and Meet. Moodle is open source and widely used by universities that host it on their own servers; it offers detailed quizzes, forums and gradebooks. Canvas is a commercial LMS with a modern interface used by many international universities. The LMS keeps a record of submission times, which matters for deadlines.

c: Lecture 9 · ICT in Education and LMS
x: A MOOC (Massive Open Online Course) is an online course open to large numbers of learners. Coursera partners with universities and companies; many courses can be audited free, with paid certificates and financial aid available. edX, founded by Harvard and MIT, offers university courses with a similar free audit model. Udemy is a marketplace where instructors sell individual courses, often at heavy discounts. Khan Academy is a non-profit offering free lessons in mathematics, science and computing, with Urdu content for some subjects. Pakistan’s own Virtual University broadcasts lectures and offers degrees through distance learning. When choosing a course, check the instructor, syllabus, reviews, duration and whether the certificate is recognised by employers.

t: L9: Interactive multimedia and virtual classrooms
c: Lecture 9 · ICT in Education and LMS
x: Interactive multimedia combines text, images, audio, video and animation with user interaction, such as simulations, educational games and quizzes. Tools like Kahoot and Quizizz turn revision into live games, Mentimeter collects instant polls, PhET simulations let students experiment with physics virtually and YouTube channels explain topics visually. A virtual classroom recreates a class online with video, chat, whiteboard, screen sharing, breakout rooms and attendance. Research on learning shows that active participation, such as answering questions and practising, improves understanding more than passively watching videos.

t: L9: Professional profiles and online learning skills
c: Lecture 9 · ICT in Education and LMS
x: LinkedIn is a professional social network where students and professionals show their education, skills, projects and certificates, connect with employers and find internships. A good profile has a professional photo, a clear headline such as ‘BS Computer Science Student | Web Development | ICT Enthusiast’, an About section, education, skills, projects and certificates from courses. Keep it honest and up to date. Success in online learning depends on self-discipline: set a weekly schedule, find a quiet place, take notes, participate in forums, avoid multitasking and keep deadlines in a calendar.

t: Lecture 9: ICT in Education and Learning Management Systems
x: Learning Management Systems (Moodle, Canvas, Google Classroom), online course platforms (Coursera, edX, Udemy, Khan Academy), interactive multimedia, virtual classrooms and building a professional LinkedIn profile. When schools and universities closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, Pakistani students experienced online learning on a large scale for the first time. Much of it was improvised, but it showed that ICT can keep education going and open doors to courses far beyond a student’s own campus. Today almost every university uses a Learning Management System, and free platforms offer courses from leading universities. This lecture explains the tools of digital education and the habits a student needs to succeed with them. E-learning can be synchronous, asynchronous or blended. An LMS delivers content, collects assignments, runs quizzes and records grades. MOOCs such as Coursera, edX, Udemy and Khan Academy widen access. Interactive tools and virtual classrooms encourage active learning. LinkedIn and disciplined study habits support academic and career growth.

Massive Open Online Course.

Smartphones and wearables such as fitness bands and smartwatches contain sensors: an accelerometer counts steps, a heart-rate sensor measures pulse and GPS records running routes. Apps such as Google Fit, Samsung Health and the Mi Fitness (Zepp) app for Mi Band store this data, show trends and set goals such as 8,000 steps a day. Some devices estimate sleep quality and blood oxygen. These numbers are estimates, useful for motivation and habits but not medical diagnoses. Health data is sensitive personal information, so review which apps can access it and whether it is shared with third parties.

Telemedicine delivers healthcare at a distance through video, audio or chat. In Pakistan, Oladoc and Marham let patients search for doctors by speciality and city, read profiles, book in-clinic or online appointments and pay online. Sehat Kahani connects patients, especially in underserved areas, with female doctors through e-clinics and an app. Benefits include saving travel time and cost, access to specialists from small towns and follow-up consultations from home. Limits include the lack of physical examination, the need for stable internet and the risk of unverified ‘doctors’ on social media. Always check that a doctor is registered with the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PM&DC).

t: L10: Digital finance: wallets, banking and payments
x: Mobile wallets such as JazzCash and Easypaisa let users send and receive money, pay utility bills, buy mobile load and pay merchants by QR code, using only a phone number and CNIC-verified account. Internet and mobile banking apps from banks let customers transfer funds, pay bills and check statements. Raast, Pakistan’s instant payment system run by the State Bank of Pakistan, allows free, instant transfers between banks and wallets using a Raast ID, usually the mobile number. Security relies on a PIN, OTPs sent by SMS and device binding. Banks and wallets never ask customers to share their PIN, OTP or full card details by call, SMS or email.

t: L10: E-commerce and safe online shopping
x: E-commerce platforms such as Daraz, Telemart and Shophive sell products from many sellers or their own stock and deliver across Pakistan. Before buying, compare prices, read recent reviews with photos, check the seller’s rating and number of orders, and read the return and warranty policy. Payment options include cash on delivery (COD), cards, wallets and bank transfer. COD reduces the risk of paying for an item that never arrives. Be careful with products advertised only on social media pages that demand advance payment, prices far below market and pressure such as ‘only 2 left’.

Common frauds in Pakistan include calls pretending to be from a bank, wallet or the Benazir Income Support Programme asking for OTPs; fake prize messages; SIM swap attempts; phishing links that copy bank login pages; and fake online shops. Protection rules: never share PIN, OTP or CVV; check the website address and padlock before entering details; enable app locks and biometric login; set SMS alerts for every transaction; use official apps from the Play Store or App Store; and report fraud immediately to your bank’s helpline and block the account or card. Cybercrime can be reported to the FIA’s cybercrime wing.

t: Lecture 10: ICT in Health, Finance and Shopping
x: Fitness tracking apps, telemedicine (Oladoc, Sehat Kahani, Marham), mobile wallets and online banking (JazzCash, Easypaisa, Raast), e-commerce (Daraz, Telemart, Shophive) and how to stay safe from fraud. Three areas of daily life have been changed by ICT more than almost any other for ordinary Pakistani families: health, money and shopping. A grandmother in a village can now consult a doctor by video, a student in Bhimber receives money from home in seconds through a mobile wallet, and a family orders school shoes online with cash on delivery. These services bring convenience but also new risks: health data privacy, fraud calls asking for OTPs and fake online sellers. This lecture covers both the use and the safe use of these tools. Fitness apps use sensors to track health habits, not to diagnose. Telemedicine connects patients to doctors remotely; verify registration. Wallets, mobile banking and Raast make payments instant. Shop safely by checking sellers, reviews and policies; COD reduces risk. Never share PIN or OTP; use official apps and report fraud quickly.
A smart device worn on the body, such as a fitness band.
Remote medical consultation using ICT.
An app that stores money and makes payments using a phone.
One-Time Password sent for verifying a transaction.
Pakistan’s instant payment system run by the State Bank of Pakistan.
A two-dimensional barcode used here for payments.
Cash on delivery: paying when the item is received.
Fraud in which a criminal obtains a duplicate of your SIM to receive your OTPs.
The use of ICT to deliver health services and information.
Financial services such as payments, transfers and banking delivered through digital channels.
Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.

t: L11: Digital identity and digital footprint
x: Your digital identity is how you appear online: your names, photos, profiles, posts and the groups you join. Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave. An active footprint is what you deliberately share, such as posts, comments and photos. A passive footprint is collected without you actively posting, such as location history, search history, cookies and app usage. Footprints are persistent (screenshots and archives last), searchable and can be seen by audiences you did not intend, such as future employers, universities and scholarship committees. Search your own name regularly to see what others can find.

Online reputation is what others think of you based on your digital footprint. Netiquette (network etiquette) is the set of polite behaviours expected online. Core rules: remember there is a human on the other side; write as you would speak face to face; avoid all capitals, which reads as shouting; respect others’ privacy by not sharing their photos or numbers without permission; check facts before forwarding; keep group chats on topic; respect time zones and working hours when messaging teachers; disagree with ideas, not people. In online classes, use your real name, mute when not speaking and use the chat appropriately.

Cyberbullying is using digital technology to repeatedly threaten, embarrass, insult or exclude someone. Forms include abusive messages, spreading rumours, creating fake profiles, sharing private photos, excluding someone from groups and online stalking. Harassment may also be sexual or blackmail-based. Victims often feel anxious and isolated because the abuse follows them home on their phones. The response steps are: do not reply in anger; take screenshots as evidence with dates; block the person; use the platform’s report tool; tell a trusted adult, teacher or counsellor; and for serious threats or blackmail report to the FIA cybercrime wing. Bystanders should support the victim and report, not share the content.

t: L11: Privacy settings and account security
x: Privacy settings control who can see your posts, profile details, friends list and contact information. On Facebook and Instagram, set the audience to Friends or a private account, limit who can find you by phone number, review tagged photos before they appear and turn off location on posts. On WhatsApp, limit who sees profile photo, last seen and about, and who can add you to groups. A strong password is long (at least 12 characters), unique for each important account and not based on personal information; a passphrase of four random words with a number and symbol is easy to remember. Two-step verification (2SV) adds a second check, usually a code from an app or SMS, so a stolen password alone is not enough. A password manager can store unique passwords safely.

Pakistan’s Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA) defines cybercrimes and penalties. Offences relevant to students include unauthorised access to someone’s account or data, identity misuse, cyberstalking, spreading sexually explicit images of a person without consent, and spoofing and fraud. The FIA’s cybercrime wing investigates complaints. The law has been amended since its introduction and some provisions are debated, so check current official sources for details. Beyond the law, digital citizens have responsibilities: respect intellectual property, protect others’ privacy and contribute positively, for example by sharing accurate information and helping others learn.

Digital identity and footprint, online reputation, netiquette, recognising and reporting cyberbullying and harassment, privacy settings, strong passwords and two-step verification, and Pakistan’s PECA 2016 framework. Citizenship means having rights and responsibilities in a community. The internet is now a community we all live in, and digital citizenship means behaving in it safely, respectfully and responsibly. For students, the stakes are real: a photo posted at sixteen can be found by an employer at twenty-five, a cruel comment can deeply hurt a classmate, and a weak password can let someone take over your social media account. This lecture moves from the tools of earlier units to the people who use them. Digital citizenship is safe, respectful and responsible technology use. Footprints are persistent; think before posting. Netiquette keeps online communication respectful. Respond to cyberbullying by saving evidence, blocking, reporting and telling someone. Use privacy settings, strong unique passwords and two-step verification; know PECA 2016.
Responsible, safe and respectful use of technology.
The trail of data left by online activity.
Polite behaviour rules for online communication.
Repeated harmful behaviour using digital technology.
A second check after the password, such as a code.
A long password made of several words.
Controls deciding who can see your information.
Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 of Pakistan.
The collection of information about a person that exists online.
The perception others form about a person or organisation from online information.
Using electronic communication to intimidate, threaten or distress another person.

c: Lecture 12 · Ethics, Copyright and Final Project
x: Intellectual property (IP) is creative work of the mind that the law protects, including writing, music, images, software, inventions and brand names. Copyright protects original creative works such as books, articles, photos, videos, music and code from the moment they are created; the owner has the right to copy, distribute, adapt and display the work. In Pakistan, copyright is governed by the Copyright Ordinance 1962 and IP matters are administered by the Intellectual Property Organisation of Pakistan (IPO-Pakistan). Other IP types include trademarks (brand names and logos) and patents (inventions). Finding an image on Google does not mean it is free to use.

t: L12: Fair use and Creative Commons
c: Lecture 12 · Ethics, Copyright and Final Project
x: Many copyright laws allow limited use of works without permission for purposes such as criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching and research, often called fair use or fair dealing. It depends on the purpose, the amount used and the effect on the original’s market, and it is not a blanket permission. Creative Commons (CC) licences let creators give permission in advance. CC BY allows use with credit; NC means non-commercial only; ND means no changes; SA means share adapted works under the same licence. CC0 places work in the public domain. Sources of openly licensed media include Wikimedia Commons, Unsplash and Pexels (check each image’s licence) and Google Images’ ‘Usage rights → Creative Commons licences’ filter.

t: L12: Plagiarism and how to avoid it
c: Lecture 12 · Ethics, Copyright and Final Project
x: Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s words, ideas, images or code as your own without proper credit. It includes copying and pasting text, paraphrasing without citation, buying or borrowing assignments, submitting the same work for two courses without permission (self-plagiarism) and copying code. Pakistani universities follow HEC’s plagiarism policy and commonly check work with similarity tools such as Turnitin; penalties range from grade reduction to cancellation of a degree. To avoid plagiarism: quote exact words in quotation marks with a citation; paraphrase by rewriting ideas fully in your own words and structure, still with a citation; summarise main points briefly with a citation; keep notes of sources while researching; and use a consistent citation style such as APA.

t: L12: AI tools and academic integrity
c: Lecture 12 · Ethics, Copyright and Final Project
x: AI writing and image tools can explain concepts, suggest outlines and check grammar, but they can also produce invented facts and references, and submitting AI-generated work as your own may break your institution’s rules. Good practice: check your teacher’s and university’s policy for each assignment; use AI to learn, not to replace your own thinking; verify every fact and reference in an original source; disclose AI assistance when required, for example ‘Grammar checked with an AI tool’; and never enter personal or confidential data into public AI tools. Your own understanding is what will be tested in exams, vivas and jobs.

c: Lecture 12 · Ethics, Copyright and Final Project
x: Misinformation is false or misleading information shared without intent to deceive; disinformation is false information spread deliberately; malinformation is true information shared to cause harm. Fake news spreads fast through WhatsApp forwards and social media because it is emotional and surprising. Verify before sharing using the SIFT approach: Stop and check your reaction; Investigate the source; Find better coverage from trusted outlets; Trace claims, quotes and images to the original context. Practical tools include Google reverse image search or Google Lens to find where a photo first appeared, checking the date and checking whether official sources confirm the claim. Be especially careful with health advice, exam leaks and emergency rumours.

t: Lecture 12: Digital Ethics, Copyright, Plagiarism, Misinformation and Final Project
x: Intellectual property and copyright, Creative Commons, plagiarism and how to avoid it with citation and paraphrasing, AI tools and academic integrity, recognising misinformation, and the Digital Portfolio final project. Throughout this course you have created documents, spreadsheets, presentations and online content, and you have used material made by others. This final lecture asks ethical questions: who owns digital work, when you may use it, how to give credit and how to avoid spreading false information. These questions matter more each year, as copying is just a right-click away and AI tools can produce text in seconds. We end by launching the Digital Portfolio, which brings together every skill from the course. Copyright protects creative works; online availability is not permission. Fair use is limited; Creative Commons grants permission with conditions. Avoid plagiarism by quoting, paraphrasing and summarising with citations. Use AI within course rules and verify its output. Use SIFT and reverse image search before sharing; complete the Digital Portfolio.

Legal right of creators over their original works.
Licences that allow reuse of works under conditions.
Works free for anyone to use without permission.
Using someone else’s work without proper credit.
Restating an idea fully in your own words.

Searching with an image to find its original source.

t: Lab 01: Identify ICT hardware, software, networks and storage
x: Every ICT system is made of hardware, software, networks and storage. Operating systems show hardware details in their settings. Local storage is attached to the device; cloud storage is reached through the internet after logging in. Complete a ‘System inventory sheet’ with three tables: (1) lab computer hardware by category, (2) software list classified as system or application, (3) network and storage details including IP address, gateway, local drive free space and cloud storage free space. Switch on the computer and log in with the lab account. Press Windows + Pause (or open Settings → System → About) and note the processor, installed RAM and Windows edition. Open File Explorer → This PC. Note each drive letter, its total size and its free space. Open Device Manager (right-click Start → Device Manager) and list one item under Keyboards, Display adapters, Network adapters and Disk drives. Open Settings → Apps and list five installed applications. Mark each as system or application software. Open Command Prompt and type ipconfig. Note the IPv4 address and Default Gateway. Explain in one line what the gateway is. Follow the network cable from your computer to the switch and note how the switch connects to the router. On your phone, open Settings → About phone and note model, Android/iOS version, RAM and storage. Create a text file named Lab01_YourName.txt with your findings so far. Save it in Documents (local). Open drive.google.com, create a folder ICT-Labs and upload the same file (cloud). Turn off Wi-Fi on the phone and try to open the file from Drive. Record what happens. Complete the comparison table and submit.

t: Lab 02: Explore ICT applications and emerging technologies
x: ICT supports education, business, governance, health and media. Emerging technologies are often already present in common apps, for example machine translation and voice typing use AI. Produce a one-page ICT scope map for your chosen field plus evidence of three hands-on activities (translation, maps traffic layer, voice typing). Open a new document named Lab02_YourName. Visit an official e-governance website (for example the NADRA or FBR site) and list two services it offers. Do not submit any personal data. Open Daraz or another shopping site and note how products are recommended under ‘You may also like’. Explain in two lines why this is AI. Open Google Translate. Translate the sentence ‘ICT is changing education in Pakistan’ into Urdu, then use the microphone to speak an Urdu sentence and record the result. Open Google Maps, search ‘Bhimber’ and turn on the Traffic layer. Note what data source makes live traffic possible (phones acting as IoT sensors). In Google Docs, try voice typing (Tools → Voice typing) for two sentences. Choose one field (education, health, agriculture, banking or media). Create a one-page ‘ICT scope map’ table: 3 tools, 3 benefits, 1 risk, 1 emerging technology for the future. Add a short reflection: which technology surprised you most? Save locally and upload to your ICT-Labs cloud folder.

t: Lab 03: Search engines, advanced searching and online research
x: Search engines rank pages; operators instruct them precisely. Reliable research uses official, academic and well-referenced sources and records where each fact came from. Complete all 10 search challenges, recording the exact query, source and answer, plus two CRAAP evaluations and two formatted references. Create Lab03_YourName with a table: Challenge | Query used | Source URL | Answer. Challenge 1: Find an exact definition of “digital divide” using quotes. Challenge 2: Find an ICT course outline in PDF: ICT course outline filetype:pdf. Challenge 3: Find an HEC page about undergraduate policy using site:hec.gov.pk. Challenge 4: Search python programming -snake and note how results change. Challenge 5: Find either Matric OR SSC result pages for BISE Mirpur. Challenge 6: Use intitle:scholarship site:edu.pk. Challenge 7: Search Google Scholar for ‘ICT in education Pakistan’ and note one paper’s title, authors, year and citation count. Challenge 8: Run challenge 2 on Bing and note one difference. Challenge 9: Pick one blog and one official page on the same topic and complete a CRAAP table for each. Challenge 10: Write two references in a consistent style (author, title, site, year, URL). Save and upload to ICT-Labs.

t: Lab 04: Email, formal communication and video conferencing
x: Formal email follows a fixed structure and uses recipient fields correctly. Calendar invitations automatically attach meeting links and reminders. Send three correctly structured emails (leave application with CC and attachment, BCC announcement, reply), set up a signature, labels and a filter, and host a 10-minute Meet session with screen sharing. Open Gmail and go to Settings → See all settings → Signature. Create a signature with name, programme, roll number and phone. Create two labels: ICT Course and Assignments. Write a leave application to the instructor (To) and a classmate (CC) with subject ‘Leave application – YourName – Date’. Attach a PDF (any sample file) and confirm it appears before sending. t: Lab 05: Microsoft Word / Google Docs document preparation
x: Styles define structure. The TOC, navigation and captions are generated from structure. PDF preserves the final layout. t: Lab 06: Microsoft Excel / Google Sheets formulas and data analysis
x: Formulas calculate from cell references; functions summarise ranges; absolute references fix constants; charts visualise patterns. Complete the Bhimber Mart analysis workbook with formulas, status flags, discount scenario, filtered Grocery sheet, sorted table and two charts. Download bhimber-mart-sales.csv from the Resources page and open it in Excel (or File → Import in Sheets). Save as Lab06_YourName.xlsx (or rename the Sheet). Add Discounted Total = Total*(1-$Discount cell$) and fill down. Change the discount to 10% and observe. Format price and total columns as currency (Rs) with no decimals. t: Lab 07: Microsoft PowerPoint / Google Slides presentation development
x: Slides use layouts and themes for consistency. Visuals and short text support the speaker; notes hold the details. Create and rehearse a six-slide ‘Mera Shehar Bhimber’ presentation with theme, Slide Master footer, image, chart, diagram, notes, one transition and limited animation, delivered within two minutes. Create a new presentation named Lab07_YourName and choose a simple theme with good contrast. Slide 1 (Title Slide): ‘Mera Shehar Bhimber’, your name and roll number. Apply one Fade transition to all slides; add an Appear animation to the SmartArt steps. Check every slide: font ≥ 28 pt for body, under 30 words, aligned elements. t: Lab 08: Cloud storage, file management, backup and sharing
x: Cloud services sync files and keep version history. Permissions control who can view, comment or edit. A consistent structure and naming makes files findable; 3-2-1 backups prevent loss. Create and share a semester folder structure, rename and upload files using a convention, demonstrate version history and Bin restore, open a file offline on your phone, create an ICT notebook and write a 3-2-1 backup plan. t: Lab 09: Learning Management Systems and online education
x: An LMS organises learning activities and records submissions and grades. MOOCs provide self-paced courses. Professional profiles showcase learning. Complete an end-to-end LMS workflow (join, discuss, quiz, submit), compare LMS features, plan a MOOC with calendar reminders and set up a LinkedIn profile. Join the instructor’s Google Classroom using the class code. Open the ‘Lab 09 Submission’ assignment and read the rubric. Post a question or comment in the Classroom Stream about any lecture topic and reply to one classmate. Take the ‘Lecture 9 Quiz’ (Google Form) attached to Classwork and note your score. t: Lab 10: ICT applications in health, finance and e-commerce
x: Health apps estimate activity using sensors; telemedicine platforms list verified doctors; e-commerce safety depends on seller evaluation and secure payment. Produce a lab report with fitness data and goal, a verified doctor profile summary, a three-listing comparison table with final choice, payment options observed (no purchase), fraud classification of three messages and a safe-payment checklist. Open a health app on your phone and note today’s steps, distance and active minutes; set a daily goal. Open Oladoc or Marham. Search for a general physician in Mirpur or Islamabad. Record the doctor’s qualification, PM&DC number if shown, fee and online consultation option. Do not book. Open Daraz and choose one product (for example a USB flash drive). Compare three listings by price, seller rating, reviews, warranty and return policy in a table. Add the best option to the cart and proceed to the payment options page only. Note available methods. Do not place the order or enter any payment details. Identify two fake-seller warning signs from social media advertisements shown by the instructor. Read three sample messages provided by the instructor and classify each as Safe or Fraud with reasons. Write a one-paragraph safe-payment checklist. Compile everything in Lab10_YourName and upload.

t: Lab 11: Digital citizenship, privacy and cybersecurity awareness
x: Footprints persist; privacy settings and strong authentication reduce exposure; netiquette and reporting reduce harm. Complete a footprint audit, before/after privacy settings table for two platforms, enable 2SV, write a password rule, respond to three scenarios and design a netiquette poster. Search your full name and username in Google; note what appears on the first page (do not include others’ private information). Open one social media account. Record five privacy settings before and after you change them: post audience, profile visibility, phone-number search, tag review, location on posts. On WhatsApp: set profile photo and last seen to My contacts and restrict who can add you to groups. Open myaccount.google.com → Security. Turn on 2-Step Verification and review recent security activity and devices. Write your personal password rule (for example ‘four words + number + symbol, unique per site’). Do not write real passwords. Optionally check your email on haveibeenpwned.com and note whether it appeared in known breaches. Read three scenario cards provided by the instructor and write the correct response steps for each. Create a one-page netiquette poster with eight rules for a class group. Compile Lab11_YourName and upload.

A digital portfolio demonstrates competence through real artefacts. Ethical practice requires attribution of media, citation of sources and appropriate sharing settings. Produce and share a complete Digital Portfolio with CV, spreadsheet, presentation, essay and README, all correctly named, cited and attributed. Create a cloud folder named ICT_DigitalPortfolio_YourName with subfolders 01_CV, 02_Excel, 03_Presentation, 04_Essay. CV: in Word/Docs create a one-page CV using styles: contact, education, skills, projects (include your labs), certificates. Export PDF. Excel: complete either a personal monthly budget or the Bhimber Mart analysis with SUM, AVERAGE, IF, an absolute reference and one chart. Presentation: five slides (About me, Skills, ICT work samples, Career goals, Thank you) with speaker notes, one CC-licensed image with attribution on the slide. Essay: write 500 words on ‘How ICT will shape my career’ with three citations and a reference list; paraphrase, do not copy. Create a README document listing every file, its purpose and all sources/licences used. Check file names follow ICT_Portfolio_Item_YourName. Share the main folder: instructor as Viewer, Restricted access; copy the link into the README. Rehearse a three-minute walkthrough of your portfolio.

t: Project 2: Excel-Based Business Management System (Bhimber Mart)
